questions.stem: Which of the following correctly defines Gross Domestic Product (GDP)?

options.option_text: Total value of goods produced by a country's citizens worldwide
Total monetary value of all goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year

questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: GDP = total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's geographic boundaries in a given period. GNP (Gross National Product) covers citizens' output worldwide. Trade balance = exports − imports (part of GDP, not its definition).

questions.stem: GVA (Gross Value Added) and GDP are related as:

options.option_text: GDP = GVA + Taxes on products − Subsidies on products

questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + Net taxes (Taxes on products − Subsidies on products). India's CSO switched to GVA-based estimation in 2015 (base year 2011-12). GVA measures output from the supply side; taxes and subsidies bridge GVA to market-price GDP.

questions.stem: Which method of GDP calculation sums the incomes of all factors of production?
questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: The Income method sums wages, rent, interest and profit (factor incomes). Expenditure method: C + I + G + (X−M). Production method: sum of value added at each stage. All three should theoretically give the same GDP — a key national accounts identity.

questions.stem: If nominal GDP rises while real GDP stays constant, it means:

options.option_text: Prices have risen (inflation) with no real output growth

questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: Real GDP is adjusted for inflation (constant prices). Nominal GDP uses current prices. If nominal rises but real stays flat: the GDP deflator (price level) has risen — only prices went up, not actual output. Real GDP growth = genuine improvement in living standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in GDP?

options.option_text: Value of household chores done by a housewife

questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: GDP counts only market transactions. Unpaid household work has economic value but is not measured in GDP because no market price is assigned. This is a well-known limitation of GDP as a welfare measure. Illegal activities and barter are also excluded.

questions.stem: The base year currently used for calculating India's GDP at constant prices is:
questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: India revised its national accounts base year from 2004-05 to 2011-12 in January 2015. The new series also shifted from GDP at factor cost to GVA at basic prices as the primary measure of activity. Base years are revised roughly every 10 years.

questions.stem: Per capita income is calculated as:
questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: Per capita income = National income (GNI or NNI) ÷ Total population. It is a rough proxy for average living standard. GDP per capita (GDP ÷ population) is also used internationally. High GDP with very unequal distribution gives high per capita income but may not reflect welfare of all citizens.

questions.stem: Which sector contributes the LARGEST share to India's GDP?
questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: Services sector (IT, banking, trade, transport, education, health) contributes ~55-60% of India's GDP. Industry ~27-28%, Agriculture ~15-17%. However, agriculture still employs ~45% of the workforce — a classic productivity gap question.

questions.stem: NDP (Net Domestic Product) differs from GDP in that:

options.option_text: NDP is measured at purchasing power parity

questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: NDP = GDP − Depreciation. Depreciation (capital consumption) is the wear-and-tear of capital goods. Net income aggregates (NDP, NNP, NNI) represent the net accretion to wealth; gross aggregates (GDP, GNP, GNI) include the replacement investment for depreciation.

questions.stem: In the expenditure method, which component is represented by 'I' in the formula Y = C + I + G + (X−M)?
questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: Y=C+I+G+(X−M): C=Private consumption, I=Gross private domestic investment (business spending on capital goods + inventory changes), G=Government expenditure, X−M=Net exports. Imports are captured in the (X−M) term, not I. Trap: confusing I with imports or income.

questions.stem: GDP at Market Prices is converted to GDP at Factor Cost by:

options.option_text: Subtracting net factor income from abroad

questions.subject: Economics
questions.explanation: GDP at Factor Cost = GDP at Market Prices − Net Indirect Taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies). Market prices include taxes (overstates factor contribution); subtracting net taxes gives the income accruing to factors of production. India now uses 'GVA at basic prices' which sits between these two concepts.
